prose: Precondition: data points to a valid YYSTACKDATA. It is spelled YYPARSE_DECL() in the source and compiled as yyparse(void); it takes tokens from yylex() and reports diagnostics through yyerror(msg). Precondition: the generated constant parse tables of this file and the lexer/error functions it calls must exist; no other state has to be initialised by the caller, because the function sets its own error count, error flag, lookahead and start state at entry; the stack structure is a file-scope static variable (allocated on first use and reused by later calls). Behaviour: it reads a token from the lexer only when no lookahead is pending (a negative lexer result is treated as end of input, token 0), shifts and reduces according to the tables, and runs the grammar's reduction actions. Its reduction actions belong to an integer calculator grammar: they print a value with printf, store into and read from the calculator registers regs[] and the number base, and compute the arithmetic results into the semantic value; rule 3 executes yyerrok (sets the error flag to 0). Syntax errors: a syntax error found while the error flag is 0 calls yyerror("syntax error") and increments the error count; an explicit YYERROR from an action (where the grammar uses it) jumps to yyerrlab, which increments the error count but does not call the error function. In recovery (error flag 3) states are popped until one shifts the error token, and lookahead tokens are discarded without further error reports. Return value: it returns 0 through yyaccept when, after reducing the start symbol, the lookahead is end of input; it returns 1 through yyabort when recovery has popped the state stack to its base without finding a state that shifts the error token, or when the lookahead is end of input while the error flag is 3; it also returns 1 (after calling yyerror("yacc stack overflow")) when yygrowstack returns YYENOMEM, because in this skeleton yyoverflow falls through into yyabort. No other value is returned. Cleanup: nothing is freed on return, because yyfreestack expands to nothing in this non-pure file; the stack stays allocated in the file-scope stack structure for the next call.

name: mainSort
prose: Static function mainSort(ptr, block, quadrant, ftab, nblock, verb, budget) of bzip2's block sorter. Precondition: nblock > 0; block and quadrant are valid for indices 0 to nblock-1+BZ_N_OVERSHOOT with block[0..nblock-1] holding the input; ptr is valid for 0..nblock-1; ftab is valid for 0..65536; budget points to a writable Int32; and the data is such that the AssertH checks with codes 1006, 1007 and 1002 hold (a failed AssertH calls the library's internal-error handler, BZ2_bz__AssertH__fail or bz_internal_error depending on the build). With verb >= 4 it prints progress text through VPrintf. Postcondition, normal return: ftab is zeroed and filled with the 2-byte frequency counts (then cumulative bucket starts) and ends with SETMASK completion bits set for the processed buckets; block[0..BZ_N_OVERSHOOT-1] is copied to block[nblock..], quadrant[0..nblock-1] is zeroed and quadrant[nblock..nblock+BZ_N_OVERSHOOT-1] is initially zeroed; ptr[0..nblock-1] is filled by the bucket distribution, by mainQSort3 on unsorted small buckets (step 1) and by the pointer scans of step 2 so that it gives the sorted order of the cyclic rotations of block (the algorithm's goal); for every big bucket except the last one processed, step 3 stores cached ordering values into quadrant (including quadrant[a2update + nblock] when a2update < BZ_N_OVERSHOOT), so the overshoot quadrant entries are not necessarily zero at the end; *budget is reduced by the work done in mainQSort3. Early return: the function returns (with no value) from step 1 immediately after a mainQSort3 call when *budget < 0, leaving ptr, ftab and quadrant partially processed; this is the only early return. It allocates and frees no memory.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: step 3 overwrites the overshoot quadrant entries (blocksort.c:995-1000: quadrant[a2update + nblock] = qVal), so the old statement that the overshoot area is left zeroed was wrong/contradictory.

name: dialog_calendar
prose: Slice cut the head: this is dialog_calendar(title, subtitle, height, width, day, month, year) (calendar.c:672). It saves the dialog variables (dlg_save_vars) and sets dialog_vars.separate_output = TRUE, takes the current local time, overrides year (>= 1900), month (>= 1) and day (valid for that month) from the arguments when given and normalises with mktime (HAVE_MKTIME build), sizes and draws the dialog window, then draws the day, month and year boxes. Return paths: if WeekStart() < 0 or init_object/DrawObject fails for any of the three boxes, it returns CleanupResult(DLG_EXIT_ERROR, ...) at once, without adding a date to the result. Otherwise it runs the key loop until result != DLG_EXIT_UNKNOWN (or until dlg_result_key reports a result key and dlg_button_key returns false): keys are mapped to button choices, field changes, date steps (day, month or year by whole-day steps through mktime/localtime), mouse selections, or a KEY_RESIZE which rebuilds the window (goto retry); the result is set from dlg_result_key, dlg_char_to_button, dlg_enter_buttoncode or dlg_ok_buttoncode. After the loop it formats the selected date with strftime and dialog_vars.date_format when that is set and produces a non-empty string, otherwise as day/month/year with the default format "%02d/%02d/%0d" (day, month, year), adds it with dlg_add_result, calls AddLastKey() and returns CleanupResult(result, ...). CleanupResult deletes the dialog window, frees the mouse regions and the prompt, restores the saved dialog variables, frees the cached day and month name strings and returns its first argument. So the date is added to the result only on the non-error path.
note: Dropped earlier only because the name was not in the slice. Two statements of the old prose were wrong: the DLG_EXIT_ERROR returns do not format/add the date ('in every case' was false), and the default date format is dd/mm/yyyy (tm_mday, tm_mon + 1, year), not mm/dd/yyyy.

name: dlg_result_key
prose: Precondition: resultp points to a writable int; dialog_key is a curses or dialog key code and fkey tells whether it came from a function-key binding. If KEY_RESIZE is defined it first updates dialog_state.had_resize: while had_resize is set, an ERR dialog_key is replaced by 0 (the local copy) and any other key clears had_resize; otherwise, if fkey is nonzero and dialog_key == KEY_RESIZE, had_resize is set. Postcondition, when the build defines HAVE_RC_FILE: for a nonzero fkey it returns TRUE and stores DLG_EXIT_OK for DLGK_OK (unless dialog_vars.nook), DLG_EXIT_CANCEL for DLGK_CANCEL (unless nocancel), DLG_EXIT_EXTRA for DLGK_EXTRA (only if extra_button is set), DLG_EXIT_HELP for DLGK_HELP (only if help_button is set) and DLG_EXIT_ESC for DLGK_ESC, and returns FALSE for every other value; for a zero fkey it returns TRUE with DLG_EXIT_ESC if dialog_key == ESC, TRUE with DLG_EXIT_ERROR if dialog_key == ERR (after the ERR-to-0 replacement above), else FALSE. When HAVE_RC_FILE is not defined the ESC and ERR tests apply for any fkey value and the function-key switch does not exist. *resultp is written only when TRUE is returned.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: without HAVE_RC_FILE the ESC/ERR checks are not guarded by fkey (dlg_keys.c:331-339), so the old unconditional statement was wrong; the original rejection (ERR not always handled because of fkey or had_resize) is also right. The prose now covers both builds.

name: dlg_form
prose: The slice is the middle of dlg_form(title, cprompt, height, width, form_height, item_no, items, current_item), the form implementation (formbox.c:463), not of the wrapper dialog_form. Precondition: items has item_no valid DIALOG_FORMITEM entries, current_item is writable, the dialog variables are initialised. It lays out the form with make_FORM_ELTs and dlg_auto_size (height or width 0 means auto size; form_height 0 means the computed height), creates the dialog window and a form sub-window, draws the box, title, prompt and field texts, picks the initial field with set_choice, and loops reading keys until result != DLG_EXIT_UNKNOWN or dlg_result_key reports a result key. In the loop: button hotkeys (when not editing text) and DLGK_ENTER/DLGK_TOGGLE set the result from dlg_ok_buttoncode/dlg_enter_buttoncode (or DLG_EXIT_OK when the state is the text field) after dlg_del_window(dialog); DLGK_LEAVE sets the result from the current button; navigation keys move between fields, buttons, pages (scrolling) or tab through items; mouse clicks select a field or set a button result; KEY_RESIZE frees the prompt, resets the size, unregisters the form window and jumps back to retry; other keys while a text field is active are passed to dlg_edit_string, which edits current->text in place unless the item is read-only. After the loop it frees the mouse regions, unregisters the form window, deletes the dialog window (dlg_del_window(dialog) is also called inside the loop in the Enter/Toggle branches before the loop ends), frees the prompt, stores the final choice in *current_item and returns result (a DLG_EXIT_* value such as DLG_EXIT_OK, DLG_EXIT_CANCEL, DLG_EXIT_ESC, DLG_EXIT_HELP, DLG_EXIT_EXTRA, DLG_EXIT_ERROR from dlg_result_key, or a button code); that return statement is the only one in the function. It does not allocate or free the items array or write the field values to the dialog output; that is done by the callers such as dialog_form.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: the old prose described the dialog_form wrapper (temporary item list, dlg_form call, output of the field texts) but the slice is dlg_form, which does none of that. The name in the packet (dialog_form) was therefore the wrong function.

name: fill_lists
prose: Precondition: current is a writable buffer of at least MAX_LEN+1 bytes holding a NUL-terminated string, input is a NUL-terminated string, d_list and f_list are initialised LISTs and keep is a bool. It finds the first position n where current and input differ. If the strings are identical it sets the result FALSE and requests a rescan only when n == 0 and d_list->length == 0 (both strings empty and the directory list empty). If they differ and neither remainder (current + n, input + n) contains '/', it does not rescan: the result is show_both_lists(input, d_list, f_list, keep), which uses the caller's keep and returns TRUE if either list's highlighted choice changed (the file list is only updated when the directory list reports no change, because of the || short-circuit). Otherwise (a '/' in either remainder) it rescans. A rescan copies input into current truncated to MAX_LEN, frees and reinitialises both lists (free_list with reinit), takes the directory part of current (or "./"), opendirs it and, when that succeeds, adds each entry of acceptable length found by stat() to d_list (directories) or, only if f_list->win is set, to f_list (other files), closes the directory and sorts non-trivial lists with qsort; if opendir fails the lists simply stay empty. It then calls show_both_lists(input, d_list, f_list, FALSE) (result ignored), sets both list offsets to their choices and the result to TRUE. Returns that result (TRUE after a rescan even if opendir failed).
note: Reviewer round 15 wrong on both points: for two empty strings with an empty directory list the code does rescan and returns TRUE (fselect.c:458-460: rescan = (n == 0 && d_list->length == 0)); FALSE is returned only for identical strings otherwise. show_both_lists is called with keep FALSE in the rescan branch and with the caller's keep in the no-slash branch, which is what the prose said. I made the keep and short-circuit details explicit.

name: digits_of
prose: Precondition: none for value (any int); the local 80-byte buffer is large enough for any int. Postcondition: returns strlen of sprintf(temp, "%d", value), the number of characters in the decimal text of value, which is the number of digits of |value| plus one when value is negative. It only uses a local buffer and has no other effects.
note: Contract assumes a 32-bit int (10 digits for INT_MAX); the earlier contract was an overlong nested conditional that did not parse. Round-1 reviewer claim (minus sign omitted) was right; later rounds were mechanical syntax rejections.

name: handle_my_getc
prose: Precondition: cb is a DIALOG_CALLBACK pointer (a MY_OBJ when it is registered), result points to a writable int. If cb is not found in dialog_state.getc_callbacks it returns FALSE and leaves *result unchanged. Otherwise, for a non-function key that dlg_char_to_button maps to button index 0 it treats the key as DLGK_ENTER. For a function key: DLGK_ENTER sets *result = DLG_EXIT_OK and done; DLGK_BEGIN sets hscroll to 0; DLGK_GRID_LEFT decrements hscroll if it is positive; DLGK_GRID_RIGHT increments it while it is below MAX_LEN; for a mouse key it sets *result = dlg_ok_buttoncode(ch - M_EVENT) (assigned even when that is DLG_EXIT_ERROR) and finishes only if the value is not DLG_EXIT_ERROR, otherwise it calls beep(); any other function key beeps. After a function key, if hscroll differs from old_hscroll it calls repaint_text. For a non-function key: ERR does clearerr(input), reads one character with getc and pushes it back with ungetc, and calls handle_input (which repaints when the file size differs from last_pos) if the character was not EOF; ESC sets *result = DLG_EXIT_ESC and finishes; any other key beeps. It returns FALSE when the dialog is finished (or the callback is not valid) and TRUE otherwise.
note: Reviewer round 15 right on both points: the invalid-callback path also returns FALSE, and the mouse path assigns *result = DLG_EXIT_ERROR before testing it (tailbox.c:264-270). The old prose also said the ERR character was consumed, but it is pushed back with ungetc, and said 'a button' matches whereas only button index 0 does.

name: find_and_hash_each_line
prose: Slice cut the head: static function find_and_hash_each_line(current) (io.c:217). Precondition: current's buffer, prefix_end, suffix_begin, buffered, linbuf, alloc_lines and linbuf_base are set up, the globals equivs, equivs_index, equivs_alloc, buckets and nbuckets are initialised (buckets[-1] must also be valid), and the options ignore_white_space, ignore_case, tabsize, output_style, context and no_diff_means_no_output are set. Behaviour: it mallocs a cureqs array of alloc_lines entries. For every line starting at prefix_end and before suffix_begin it hashes the line text (honouring ignore_case and ignore_white_space: IGNORE_ALL_SPACE, IGNORE_SPACE_CHANGE, IGNORE_TAB_EXPANSION), looks for an equal line in the hash bucket (same hash, then memcmp or lines_differ) and otherwise adds a new equivalence class to eqs (growing it by doubling with xrealloc; xalloc_die if the size would exceed PTRDIFF_MAX), stores the line start in linbuf[line] and the class index in cureqs[line] (growing linbuf and cureqs by doubling when full), and counts lines; an incomplete last line is put in buckets[-1] when whitespace is significant and the buffer end is moved back over the inserted newline. It then sets current->buffered_lines to that count. A second loop records line starts for the lines of the suffix, one start per line plus one extra entry for the end (bufend, or the start of the line at which it stops once context lines have been recorded when no_diff_means_no_output is set), growing linbuf as needed. Finally it stores linbuf, valid_lines (the index of that last entry), alloc_lines and cureqs (as current->equivs) in current and the local equivalence table, size and index back into the globals equivs, equivs_alloc and equivs_index. It returns nothing; allocation failure or size overflow ends the process through xalloc_die.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: linbuf gets one extra start entry (the end sentinel) beyond the lines (io.c:468-496), which the old prose omitted. Dropped-name issue: the packet name matches the real function; the slice just starts after its head.
